message.content:
In lions, one of the most striking examples of a dominant genetic trait is the **presence of a mane in adult male lions**. The mane is a secondary sexual characteristic that is largely governed by a dominant allele (often referred to as the “mane” allele). While the exact genetic locus has not been fully mapped, studies suggest that:

1. **Dominant Allele (M)** – When present, it leads to the development of a mane.  
2. **Recessive Allele (m)** – When homozygous recessive (mm), the lion will not develop a mane.

Because the mane is a visible, sexually selected trait, it has been a focus of evolutionary and genetic research. In practice, this means that if a male lion inherits at least one copy of the dominant allele from either parent, he will develop a mane; only if he inherits two copies of the recessive allele will he remain mane‑less.
